title: Suzuki Roshi's Compassion
speaker: Ryushin Andrea Thach
summary: Ryushin Andrea Thach reflects on their experience at Tassajara Monastery, where they studied calligraphy and communed with nature, drawing inspiration for exploring the concept of compassion in relation to emptiness. They note that true freedom comes from letting go of attachments and desires, as exemplified by Suzuki Roshi's journey towards compassion after recognizing his own suffering. This understanding is rooted in the idea that compassion arises from embracing emptiness and interconnectedness, allowing us to be present and supportive in the face of difficulties, both within ourselves and for others.

sentences.text: Good evening, everyone.
I've only been gone a week.
It's already gotten to be winter.
Well, it's a particular privilege to be here tonight and have the opportunity to speak, having just arrived back after a week away at Tassajara.
Tassajara Zen Mountain Monastery is the monastery for our particular lineage.
It's in the Carmel Valley Ventana Wilderness in Central California.
So I was there for a week studying calligraphy and communing with the land and the monks there.
I wanted to bring back a little bit of that visit here in some way, and I'm going to try something that's a little different and spontaneous, and we'll see how that goes.
I'm talking about as loud as I can.
If you can't hear me well, please come up closer.
You can come up over here, bring your chair, scoot up.
This is about as loud as I think I can get tonight.
The title of this talk is something like Suzuki Roshi's Compassion.
I wanted to talk too about Shunryu Suzuki Roshi, who was the founder of San Francisco Zen Center and the Dharma grandfather of the founder of this temple, Norman Fischer.
We just finished a month's study of him, and it was a wonderful opportunity for me to revisit his teachings more deeply.
So I wanted to bring some of that forward too, integrating that with the experience of what it is to be at Tassajara.
Has anyone here been to Tassajara?
Some are going again soon.
I've been fortunate enough over the last 20 years to make a number of trips.
I think one often has a first impression arriving there.
It's a place of great beauty.
It's a place of incredible peace and settledness.
You get the immediate sense that it's some place, not to use too heady a word, sacred.
It was native land and a native sacred spot.
There are hot springs there, long before people came and made it into a dude ranch.
And then something else before it was purchased in the early to mid-1960s by San Francisco Zen Center.
The first time I went there, as a very new, not fully rooted Zen student, what I felt was a place of great refuge.
I immediately knew it was some place I wanted to be.
There's a feeling there that the practice, the years of practice, are somehow worn into the landscape, into the patina of what it is to walk around there.
If you can imagine, it's down a steep valley, 14 miles down a very unimproved road.
The hillsides are very, very tall, so it stays cold and dark until about 10.
And then it gets cold and dark again by about 5.
This is in a late summer afternoon.
It's a place where three creeks come together.
In the first practice period I did, the Zendo is along one of those creeks, and it sounded like the BART tracks in San Francisco going by, the water was flowing so heavily.
It was phenomenal.
And over the years there have been all kinds of birds.
For those of us who love birds and trees and coyotes and cougars and bobcats and deer, it's a very bountiful place.
At night in practice periods, when you walk back from the Zendo with the lanterns lit, you can feel the spirits of the native people in certain areas.
Everyone says they've seen ghosts actually come into the Zendo.
And I'll attest to that experience one night when I was sleeping in the Zendo before I had to get up early to light the lanterns.
Just to give you some sense of the place.
This time, this trip, somehow I was taken by the stones, by the geology of the place, and particularly by the rocks.
The stonework has always been quite beautiful.
I'm going to talk about that a little bit because that was one of Suzuki Roshi's practices with his students.
I don't know if it's because the last fire that burned there burned down some of the vegetation enough that, with the rains that came two years ago, a lot of the stones washed down from the hillside.
Or because the creeks are bone dry in most places now, after the drought and all the heat that we've had.
But somehow there were stones everywhere.
It's like people had been finding them and taking them and stacking them up in different places.
There's always been stonework, but I swear they were propagating.
What's phenomenal is how beautiful these stones all are.
They're so different.
They're the big river rocks that are gray and white and worn into different patterns, soothed.
It's glacial in part, it's volcanic in part, it's sedimentary, it's conglomerate.
You'll find all of that in the same patches, in a range of colors that go from blues to reds to grays to tans.
In these rocks.
In these rocks.
In these rocks.

In these rocks, it is possible, I felt, the centuries of life that were there, that are manifest in the minerals of these rocks, that are manifest in the life forms that were compressed together to make these lives.
I felt the aliveness of these rocks and the spirit in them and the way the earth manifests all of the life that's been there, here and now in this moment.
It's almost like they were talking or singing.
Just singing, vibrating in their energy.
So beautiful.
Dogen writes in the Mountains and Waters Sutra of mountains walking.
Mountains do walk.
Have no doubt that the Blue Mountains walk.
This may not make any sense to you, but there actually is a little method to what I'm doing.
There are transcripts of Suzuki Roshi's lectures.
Many of them were given at Tassajara in what is now used as a student dining room in the summertime.
It's screened off.
It's not used much in the winter during practice period.
It's too cold.
But in that place, with lit lanterns, he would sit and talk, and there would be wonderful exchanges with his students.
These are all transcribed and archived.
A very few of them are in the collections of books that we have, but all of them are online.
This is an exchange with a student 50 years ago, 1968, November 11th.
*[unclear: "Doucho Roshi"].
Very often I feel your compassion.
I don't understand emptiness.
I was wondering where compassion is in emptiness.*
*Suzuki Roshi: Compassion.*
*Student: What is emptiness?*
*Suzuki Roshi: Compassion will be directed, will be on always some phenomenal world, which can cause our attachment.
Originally everything is empty.
That is how our compassion arises.
So compassion and somethingness and emptiness is the same.
Has the same quality.
When we understand compassion, emptiness, we become compassionate on something which exists in terms of material or spiritual.
So emptiness is not different from compassion.
It is the source of compassion.*
*Student: I'm not sure I understand, but I don't know.
I don't know what to say about my not understanding.
I can't ask another question.*
*Suzuki Roshi: When there is something, there should be compassion.
When there is something, there should be compassion.
Compassion should always be on every being.
Like everything arises from emptiness.*
I find Suzuki Roshi's path in his life quite phenomenal.
I thought a lot about how he became the teacher that he became.
You're here tonight in part because he was the teacher that he was.
He had great, great difficulties in his life.
He somehow transformed them.
They weren't impediments.
He had very strict training from a very young age.
In Japan, he lived through the war.
There was starvation.
People suffered terribly.
There was a spirit in Japan that they had to fight no matter what, even when people knew that they were going to lose.
Suzuki Roshi took a very rigid stand with himself.
He said, if Dogen's teaching is true, I shouldn't have to go to work like the other priests are doing to survive in the war.
I'm just going to do my practice.
And phenomenally, he said, I'm going to test Dogen.
And phenomenally, he did.
He worked in the garden.
He made food available to people in the community who had none.
And when he ran out, they brought him some.
Slowly, the community came together to make enough food.
People came to him for instruction.
Even the young military who were going off to fight the war came for instruction.
And he was a pacifist in the instruction he gave.
He started a preschool, instructed young women.
He was actually fairly radical in what he did.
Before the war, he had been married once.
His young wife quickly became ill with tuberculosis.

And it was determined, not by Suzuki Roshi but by those around him, that she would never be well enough to take on the rigors of being a temple wife, which of course was going to be his destination, to be a temple priest.
And so the marriage was annulled.
It wasn't a choice Suzuki Roshi made.
It's one he assented to because it was required.
He married a second time and had three children.
He was married for 18 years.
And again, his stubbornness was an impediment.
He was asked by one of his teachers to take on a very troubled monk.
And he couldn't say no.
He was quite proper about it.
That troubled monk made his children and his wife very uncomfortable.
He probably had some kind of serious condition.

One time when Suzuki Roshi was away attending a funeral or the needs of someone in the community, this monk had some kind of crazy experience and attacked the family dog who was barking, with a knife, killing it.
Then he turned on the wife, who tried to stop him, stabbing her fatally in front of the children.
You can only imagine what it was like for him to bear that truth of what his stubbornness, his insensitivity, his unwillingness to listen to his wife, what tragedy that meant for his family.
He had great difficulties.
I wondered, how did he ever resolve that?
Recognizing his errors, making great apology and turning towards his suffering and the suffering he created, deeply.
And it was only a few years later, six years later, that he was given the opportunity to fulfill a life stream, which was to go to America.
Somehow he always intuited that he wanted to go to America.
Kind of like Jane Goodall, who knew from a very young age that she wanted to work with apes.
Somehow she knew that when she was a young girl.
Sometimes people have an early calling, and they know it.
They know what that is.
Somehow he knew for himself.
When we restrict ourselves by what we want or what we think we want, we restrict ourselves by what we want or what we think we want.
He had some idea, and he let go of it and followed his impulse to go to America.
He says:
*We should not be caught by anything.
Until you have had that kind of strength or freedom, you should practice hard.
The purpose of practice is not to chase after worldly freedom, but it is to have freedom from our small desires or fame or success in our mundane world.
And if possible, to help people, to release them from the kind of mundane wishes and restrictions.
That is Buddhist way of life.
Join you in your path in your ordinary life, and then you have freedom from ordinary life.
There is a big difference.*
To not be caught by anything, even our difficulties.
To turn toward our difficulties so as not to be caught by them.
The stones in Tassajara have a long history.
They began with Suzuki Roshi as a young boy, docho, as a young boy training with his first teacher.
The first teacher was a master of working with stones.
He built stone walls, he built stone houses, and Suzuki Roshi learned how to work with those stones himself as a young boy.
And when they arrived at Tassajara, there was a lot to be built and a lot of stones around.
So part of what they did together is that they moved these stones, they built these walls.
The walkway is probably a half mile long.

There are stone walls along the creeks, there are stone walls to build the zendo, there are stone walls to build the kitchen, there are stone walls to create the paths, and they built all of those together.
And he, at this point, he's in his early 60s, and probably not a whole lot bigger or taller than I am, maybe a little bit.
And he was moving those stones with them.
Teaching them how to listen to the stones, teaching them how to move the stones, himself moving big stones.
There are two stories.
There's one of him working with two big, most of them were young, you know, '60s hippies, big, young, strong guys.
And one of them was an all-American football player, Phil Wilson from Stanford.
Two of these guys were trying to break a stone in order to use it in something.
They spent a day with whatever you use, a great big hammer and a chisel, and they're whacking it with this mallet, trying to break it.
At the end of the day, they've chipped out a couple of places from the top.
Then Suzuki Roshi comes along, and he spends some time feeling the rock.
I can imagine him almost climbing on it, feeling the rock and trying to get a sense of it.
And he says to them, "Right here."
And you know what happens.
Take the mallet and whack!
With a couple of hits, it splits wide open.
Another story is they're trying to move another rock into place.
They spend two days and they haven't budged it.
They're down in one of the creek beds.
They haven't budged it.
Someone yells down at them, "What are you doing down there?"
Suzuki Roshi looks up and he says, "We don't know!"
Everything we do, everything we touch, has life in it.
How we care for them arises out of emptiness.
Yvonne Rand, who is Suzuki Roshi's main assistant, tells a wonderful story that happened at San Francisco Zen Center, which is in a very urban area.
Back in those days there were a lot of street people and a lot of street activity.
It's the '60s, so you can imagine there was a lot going on, and people were in many different states in that neighborhood.
At some point, a young man somehow appears and gets into the building, and he's very agitated.
He's creating discomfort.
Maybe he's talking to himself and he's behaving kind of erratically.
Yvonne describes herself as the director, looking out and wondering what to do, and some of the other senior people are too.
You can imagine Reb Anderson and Richard Baker as younger people at that point in time, thinking, okay, how are we going to handle this?
And Suzuki Roshi walks up to him in a very friendly way and connects with him very directly and begins talking with him, just talking to him in a regular way.
I'm not sure this young man was talking in a way we would consider very regular, but Suzuki Roshi was just talking with him in a very regular way.
In a very slow, steady way, but not forceful, he walks him to the door.
Five or ten minutes later he's at the door and he just smiles at him and escorts him out in total harmony, just taking care of what needed to be taken care of.
Think of how much can be accomplished when there's no aversion, when there's no turning away from suffering, when there's meeting with the reality of what's happened, whatever it is that's happened.
One of his favorite, famous sayings is that "in the mind of experts there are few possibilities, but in the beginner's mind there are many."
So the question is how to have compassion.
It arises out of what we call emptiness, and emptiness is really something very simple.
It's simply not knowing.
It's simply not creating what isn't there.
It's simply allowing what it is to be, to be whatever it is, to come forward, to create itself, to be a part of that creation.
That's the expression of emptiness, to have a don't-know mind.
That's the expression of compassion, to not know, to be totally present, to be quite willing.
When there's a vividness and clarity about what's important, you know what to do.
It's not troubled by your sense of yourself, of attachment, of wanting something.
Compassion naturally arises out of that.
When you know what's in your heart, what's important, then you can give it freely.
As he says again:
*So when you have real freedom from everything, you may be very sympathetic with people who are involved in small personal desires, and to be involved in competitive world.
So naturally you want to help people to be free, free from this kind of life.
To share the joy of freedom with purpose is our purpose in life.
Usually people are deeply involved in city life, and so they stay in city.
But Buddhists remain in the city and live in city to help people who are involved in this kind of confusion.*
*The way upward, that means the way up the mountain in practice.* It's the idea of going to the monastery.
*The way upward is to make ourselves free from small self-desires.
And the way downward is after we have that kind of freedom to help people.
And to go back to the city is the way downward.
So, after you have your freedom, you do not enjoy the freedom around because you feel there's suffering in your heart.
And you cannot help going back to the city to help people.*
He's saying because you feel the suffering in their heart.
What he means by "enjoy the freedom," he means you can't just sit back and have a good time with it: "I'm free, I'm not troubled by anything.
It's all cool.
I think I'll just go and enjoy the good life now."
He's not saying you don't feel some kind of deep joy, some kind of deep ease.
You do.
But what he's saying is you don't keep it all for yourself.
You just naturally want to offer up because you have a profound sensitivity, a profound openness to the suffering of others.
*That's the way downward, way upward.
You should go down one flight again.
Go closer to the suffering.
Don't turn away from it.
Whether you are a priest or layman, you should.
You should start our practice from actual experience.*
So, the stones.
I've never been in Tassajara when it's been so dry.
It was really very startling.
That's part of why the rocks spoke so loudly.
There was no water covering any of them in the stream beds.
Almost none.
A few little places, and it was quickly drying up.
The deer who were always hiding in the daytime were freely wandering in parts of the community where you had to cross to get to the one little section that had water.
Imagine.
And I was walking to cross the creek bed to go on a favorite trail when I realized I could walk in the creek.
And so I started to walk along the creek on all these great big beautiful rocks.
A young woman came from around the corner where the creek turned.
She came along the rocks from the other direction and we met.
Tassajara has magic.
People are so affected by its stillness and presence, its beauty, its aura, that there's an openness that people share so readily.
It's quite magical.
You know how sometimes you have experiences where there's a synchronicity, or things just fall into place.
So it's very intimate at Tassajara.
Very intimate.
She came up to me.
I'd never seen her before.
I didn't have the sense that she was someone who was a regular practitioner.
It's guest season.
Many people come because it's a beautiful place.
Maybe they have some interest in meditation or have sat a few times or something.

She came up to me and she said she'd been walking the creek bed and that she had watched as a couple of fish had breathed their last breaths as the water was drying up around them and the algae that's there was taking up all the oxygen.
And so she watched as they ended their lives.

We shared the moment together in this beautiful place, feeling the life of this beautiful place in the rocks and in the drying hillsides and the trees that have been given a reprieve from the hard rains two years ago.

We recognized the ineffableness of all of this, of all our lives, and particularly now this precious earth, whose finiteness, given circumstances, we sometimes can imagine, in a way that when I was growing up would have been unforeseeable, thousands of years, if not more, off.
And we said yes, and us too.
Someday we too may well be like fish.
We just held that moment in this most beautiful way that recognizes that that's what life is, whether it's the phenomena of global warming or whether it's just the natural process of things.
That's emptiness.
That's compassion.
To not turn away but to accept the evanescent beauty of this life and the fact that we're all stuck in it.
*Compassion will be directed, will be on always some phenomenal world which caused our attachment.
Originally everything is empty.
That is how our compassion arises.
So compassion and somethingness and emptiness is the same, has same quality.
When we understand compassion emptiness we become compassionate on something which exists in terms of material or spiritual.
So emptiness is not different from compassion.
It is source of compassion.*
That's what I have to say.
And I wonder if you have any thoughts or questions or reflections about this, or Suzuki Roshi, anything else?
There are those striations in that sedimentary rock.
You want to pass it around?
It gives you some idea of the complexity of the rocks there.
I don't know, is anybody else taking geology?
**Participant:** I think you have just like a billion year old rock right there instead of a million year old rock.
By the time a sedimentary rock starts finding its friends, the basalts are finding their friends.
I don't know what the white guy is, but they start separating themselves into striations.
You are talking, I mean this looks like the Canadian shield, but the Canadian shield is pink and white stripes.
You picked a gorgeous one, you went right to it.
There are so many of them.
I think it would be a field day.
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** A friend of mine who is a geologist is also a Zen priest and he said this is an amazing place geologically.
**Participant:** The fact that you are talking about volcanic rocks in the same area.
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** Yes, and if you look at the mountain sides you will see that there is this kind of movement and different striations of rock there, maybe from the earthquake activity.
Faults, are there also faults?
**Participant:** There are also faults, yeah.
Check this one out with your friend because I think you have just, I mean this is like.
Give it back.
I don't want it.
Uh-oh, there is a tattoo.
I've been making a show for a long time.
That is where the three billion year old piece of raw planet is showing up there.
That is very cool.
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** Maybe sometime we will go for a walk.
Well, we are over time.
I was going to extract more comments out of you because I can imagine you have some thoughts.
It is too late.
Thank you very much for listening.
Thank you very much.
